name: Acetyl tetrapeptide-15

lead: Acetyl tetrapeptide-15 is a cosmetic peptide marketed under the name Skinasensyl for easily irritated skin. It is a minor ingredient, found in about 2 of 88 sensitive-skin products surveyed.
Its supporting evidence is a supplier cell study and a 20-person capsaicin test; a 2021 review found no peer-reviewed publications on it.

paras: It is described as derived from endomorphin-2 and as acting on mu-opioid receptors to dampen sensory nerve signalling, indirectly reducing TRPV1 responses and CGRP release.
No specific adverse events are reported; the review cites supplier safety data. It is a cosmetic ingredient, not a medicine.

web.title: Usage of Synthetic Peptides in Cosmetics for Sensitive Skin (PMC full text)

lead: Acetyl tetrapeptide-15, sold by its supplier under the trade name Skinasensyl, is a synthetic peptide used in cosmetics aimed at sensitive or reactive skin. A 2021 review describes it as derived from endomorphin-2, a mu-opioid receptor agonist, and proposes that it raises the excitability threshold of skin sensory nerves in an endorphin-like way [1].

Supplier-reported work cited in that review includes an in vitro finding that the peptide reduced release of the neuropeptide CGRP from sensory neurons, an effect weakened by the opioid blocker naloxone, and a split-face study in 20 people reporting a higher capsaicin discomfort threshold after four days of use [1]. The same review states that no studies of the compound were found in the scientific literature, only a patent and supplier documents [1].
It appears in a small share of sensitive-skin products: about 2.3 percent of 88 facial cosmetics analysed in the review [1]. It is not a drug and has no approved medical use.
infobox: Mu-opioid receptor, indirect effect on TRPV1 signalling [1]

paras: According to the review, activation of mu-opioid receptors is thought to reduce the response of the heat and capsaicin sensor TRPV1 by lowering adenylate cyclase signalling and protein kinase A phosphorylation [1]. In neuron cultures at 0.001 percent, the peptide reportedly lowered CGRP release, and the effect was reduced by naloxone, which the review reads as consistent with opioid-receptor binding [1].

The one human study cited in the review is a supplier-reported, single-blind, split-face test in 20 volunteers using a 0.0015 percent solution twice daily for four days, which reported a significantly higher capsaicin discomfort threshold [1]. The review notes that no peer-reviewed publications on the compound were found [1]. No independent trials in people with diagnosed skin conditions were found.

The review states that such peptides are regarded as safe for topical use on the basis of supplier safety data sheets and Cosmetic Ingredient Review assessments, and it reports no specific adverse events [1].
No community discussion of this ingredient was identified; it appears mainly in ingredient lists of sensitive-skin products.
